prerequisites: Electricity and Magnetism: Electrical circuits: basic laws (Kirchhoff) and defining equations of elements.
Mathematics I: Vector calculus and operation with complex numbers; trigonometry; knowledge and use of exponential and logarithmic functions.
Mathematics II: Resolution of systems of linear equations and second-degree equations.

Mathematics III: Differential and integral calculus (concepts of derivation and integration, derivative and integral of simple functions); Differential equations and resolution of differential equations; Laplace transforms and application to the resolution of differential equations.
Mechanics: Concepts of torque, speed, power, rotational systems, linear systems and associated basic laws of dynamics.
Basic knowledge imparted in Mathematics and in the Electricity and Magnetism course.

learning_outcomes.text: Know the fundamentals of circuit theory.
Know, understand and be able to apply the principles of circuit analysis.
Understand and be able to apply the modeling techniques typical of circuit theory.
Be able to identify and describe the behavior of electrical components.
Know the fundamentals of electrical machines.
Understand and be able to apply the principles of circuit theory to electrical machines.
Be able to make approximations to engineering problems related to electrical circuits and machines.

syllabus_topics: PART ONE - Topic 1. Elements of electrical circuits - 1.1 Ideal active and passive elements. - 1.2. Real active and passive elements. - 1.3. Relationship between voltage and current in electrical elements. - 1.4. Association of elements and source conversion. - 1.5. Circuit topology.
Topic 2. General methods of circuit analysis. - 2.1. Nodal equation based methods. - 2.2. Loop equation based methods.
Topic 3. Fundamental theorems. - 3.1. Superposition theorem. - 3.2. Thevenin's and Norton's theorems. - 3.3. Rosen's theorem. - 3.4. Maximum power transfer theorem.

Topic 4. Circuits in sinusoidal steady state. - 4.1. Series RLC circuit. - 4.2. Parallel RLC circuit. - 4.3. Power and energy in electrical elements in sinusoidal alternating current. - 4.4. Active, reactive and apparent powers. - 4.5. Complex power. - 4.6. Power factor of an installation. - 4.7. Power factor improvement. - 4.8. Resonant circuits. - 4.9. Two-port networks: Quadripoles.

PART TWO - Topic 5. Polyphase systems. - 5.1. Generation of a polyphase voltage system. - 5.2. Three-phase systems. - 5.3. Balanced three-phase circuits. - 5.4. Unbalanced three-phase circuits. - 5.5. Power measurement in three-phase circuits.
Topic 6. Introduction to transient regime in electrical circuits. - 6.1. Circuits in the transformed field. - 6.2. First-order circuits. - 6.3. Second-order circuits.

Topic 7. Introduction to electrical machines and lines. - 7.1. General aspects of electrical machines. - 7.2. Principles of electromechanical energy conversion. - 7.3. Most used parameters and characteristics in electrical machines. - 7.4. The electrical system. - 7.5. Introduction to electrical installations.

LABORATORY PRACTICES. - Practice 1. Circuit analysis 1. Sinusoidal voltages and currents. - Practice 2. Circuit analysis 2. Study of a series and parallel RLC circuit, powered by a single-phase AC. - Practice 3. Circuit analysis 3. Verification of fundamental circuit theorems. - Practice 4. Circuit analysis 4. Measurement and improvement of power factor in single-phase receivers. - Practice 5. Two-port networks. Electrical Quadripoles. - Practice 6. Three-phase systems 1. Measurement of voltages and currents in three-phase alternating current circuits, with balanced three-phase receivers. - Practice 7. Three-phase systems 2. Measurement of voltages and currents in three-phase alternating current circuits, with unbalanced three-phase receivers. - Practice 8. Three-phase systems 3. Measurement of powers and power factor in three-phase alternating current circuits, with balanced and unbalanced three-phase receivers. - Practice 9. Study of circuits in transient regime. - Practice 10. Introduction to electrical machines and connection to the LV network.
assessment_rules: To pass the course, the final grade must be at least 50% of the total value (a score of 5 out of 10 points). A minimum of 40% must be obtained in each block of the final written exam, and their average must be at least 4.5 out of 10 points. The grade from lab reports will only be averaged into the final grade if the grade for this assessment system is greater than 50% of its total value. If this critical evaluation criterion is not met, the total course grade will be a FAIL, with the resulting sum of all grades truncated to a maximum of 4.5 points.
